subject: security
title: Applied Cryptography & PKI
summary: How the primitives become real systems: digital signatures, certificates and chains of trust, how TLS combines everything, key management with KMS and HSMs, end-to-end encryption in the Signal protocol, and the mistakes and post-quantum changes that shape modern crypto engineering.

lessons.title: What signatures prove
lessons.summary: A signature separates signing authority from public verification; a shared-key MAC does not.
lessons.body:
A **digital signature** lets a signature verifier with a trusted public key check message integrity and authenticity to the corresponding signing key, under the scheme's security assumptions. It does not identify a human or establish freshness by itself.

Message authentication codes (MACs), introduced in cryptographic primitives, authenticate with a shared secret. MACs also prove integrity and origin, but both sides share the same secret key, so either side could have produced the tag. A signature splits the key in two. Holders of the private key can sign; anyone with the public key can verify. That asymmetry is what makes signatures useful between strangers, and it is the foundation of certificates, software updates and TLS.

## What a signature scheme is

Every signature scheme is three algorithms:

1. **KeyGen** produces a key pair: a private signing key `sk` and a public verification key `pk`.
2. **Sign(sk, message)** produces a signature, a short string of bytes.
3. **Verify(pk, message, signature)** returns true or false.

The security goal is called **existential unforgeability under chosen-message attack** (EUF-CMA). Even after obtaining signatures on chosen messages, an efficient attacker should have only negligible probability of producing a valid signature on a message not previously submitted for signing, under the scheme's assumptions.

| Property | MACs | Signatures |
|---|---|---|
| Keys | One shared secret | Private + public |
| Who can create | Anyone with the key | Private key holder |
| Who can verify | Anyone with the key | Anyone |
| Signature verifier can check without signing power | No (shared key) | Yes |
| Speed | Usually lower computational cost | Cost depends on scheme and operation |

Signatures can support evidence of origin because verification need not grant signing authority. Attribution also needs trustworthy identity binding, key custody and protocol context. This lesson makes no legal claim: a valid signature alone does not prove that a particular person acted, and its weight in a dispute depends on the jurisdiction and the other evidence.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A shared office stamp versus a signet ring
> Two business partners share one rubber stamp. A stamped letter shows that one of them stamped it, but not which one. Compare that with a signet ring that only one person wears, where everybody has been given a reference impression of the ring to compare against.
>
> **How it maps:** The shared stamp is a MAC key: every holder can both create and check a tag, so the tag cannot single out its maker. The ring is the private signing key and the reference impression is the public verification key: checking a signature never gives you the power to make one.
>
> **Where it stops:** A wax impression can be copied onto another letter and judged by eye. A digital signature covers the exact bytes it was made over, so changing a single bit makes verification fail, and the check is mathematical rather than visual. You must also trust that the reference impression really belongs to the ring's owner, which is the job of certificates.

> [!warning] Signing is not encrypting
> A signature alone does nothing for confidentiality: its message may remain readable unless separately encrypted. If both are needed, use a suitable authenticated-encryption protocol. TLS certificate handshakes use signatures for authentication; Signal's message protection is not simply a publicly verifiable signature on every message.

## Hash, then sign

Many signature schemes hash messages as part of their encoding, but the construction is scheme-specific. For example, pure Ed25519 hashes the message together with secret-derived material and signature/public-key data; it is not simply Sign(SHA256(message)). Follow the API's message or prehash interface. The diagram is only a simplified hash-then-sign construction.

```
simplified hash-then-sign example
message
     |
  SHA-256
     |
 32-byte digest --Sign(sk)--> signature
```

This is why hash **collision resistance** matters so much. If an attacker can find two documents with the same hash, a signature on the harmless one is also a valid signature on the harmful one. That is exactly how researchers forged a rogue CA certificate using MD5 collisions in 2008, and why SHA-1 was retired from certificates, a decision vindicated by the SHAttered collision in 2017.

## Key takeaways
- A signature separates signing authority from public verification; a shared-key MAC does not.
- Signatures authenticate bytes to a key, without hiding the message or proving a human identity.
- Message hashing and encoding belong to the specified scheme; collisions can undermine digest-only signing.

## Further reading
- [RSA signature schemes — RFC 8017](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017)
- [EdDSA — RFC 8032](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032)
- [Deterministic ECDSA — RFC 6979](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6979)

questions.prompt: A payments API and merchant share an HMAC key. Can the tag alone distinguish which party created a webhook, and how does an asymmetric signature change verification authority?

options.text: HMAC-SHA256 is too weak to be admissible; HMAC-SHA512 would fix it
options.explanation: Hash length is not the issue. Any HMAC, however strong, is computed with a key both sides hold, so it cannot single out one of them.

options.text: The API should encrypt the webhook body so only the merchant can read it
options.explanation: Encryption gives confidentiality, not attribution. Signing is not encrypting, and encrypting is not signing.

options.text: Either shared-key holder can create the tag; a signature lets a signature verifier check without holding the signing key
options.explanation: Correct. This separates verification from signing authority. It does not by itself establish human authorship or the legal result of a dispute.

options.text: HMACs cannot be verified by anyone, so the API should send the key with each message
options.explanation: Sending the key would let anyone forge tags. The merchant can already verify the HMAC; the problem is that it can also *create* one.

questions.workedExample: Both holders can compute the same HMAC, so it cannot distinguish them. A signature verifier only needs a public key, which does not normally grant signing authority. Attribution still depends on trusted key binding and custody; no legal conclusion follows from this example alone.

questions.prompt: A team signs every message in their internal queue with Ed25519 and concludes the payloads are now protected from anyone sniffing the network. What is wrong with that conclusion?

options.text: Nothing; Ed25519 signatures hide the payload
options.explanation: A signature is computed over the message, which is still sent alongside it in the clear. Signatures provide no confidentiality.

options.text: Ed25519 signatures can be stripped, so they provide no integrity
options.explanation: Stripping a signature is noticed if the receiver requires one. Integrity is exactly what signatures *do* give.

options.text: Ed25519 is only for TLS certificates and cannot sign arbitrary messages
options.explanation: Ed25519 signs arbitrary byte strings; it is used for SSH keys, Git, packages and tokens as well as certificates.

options.text: Signatures give integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality; they still need encryption such as TLS
options.explanation: Correct. Anyone on the network can read signed messages. If secrecy matters, they also need encryption, ideally a protocol like TLS that combines both correctly.

questions.workedExample:
Ask what each primitive guarantees:

| Primitive | Gives |
|---|---|
| Encryption | Confidentiality |
| MACs | Integrity, origin (shared) |
| Signature | Integrity, origin (public) |

The sniffer cannot *change* a signed message without detection, but can read every byte. To stop reading, encrypt as well.

questions.prompt: For a construction that signs only a specified message digest, and the historical examples below, which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: If two documents have the same hash, a signature on one is a valid signature on the other
options.explanation: Correct. The signature covers only the digest, so colliding documents share signatures. This is why collision resistance is essential.

options.text: Hashing first is mainly done for confidentiality
options.explanation: The hash is not secret and the message is sent anyway. Hashing is for fixed size and speed, plus it feeds the padding scheme.

options.text: MD5 collisions were used in 2008 to create a rogue CA certificate
options.explanation: Correct. Researchers obtained a CA-signed certificate whose MD5 hash collided with a CA certificate they controlled.

options.text: A longer message produces a longer signature
options.explanation: The signature is over a fixed-size digest, so its length depends on the algorithm and key, not the message.

options.text: SHA-1 was retired from certificate signing, and a practical SHA-1 collision (SHAttered) was published in 2017
options.explanation: Correct. The CA/Browser Forum phased out SHA-1, and the SHAttered collision confirmed the decision.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each claim:

1. Signing the hash: equal hashes mean equal inputs to the signing operation, so the signature transfers. True.
2. Hashing gives a fixed-size input and avoids slow public-key operations over large data. It hides nothing. False.
3. The 2008 rogue CA attack used an MD5 chosen-prefix collision. True.
4. Signature size is fixed: 64 bytes for Ed25519, 256 bytes for RSA-2048. False.
5. SHA-1 was retired and SHAttered showed a real collision. True.

lessons.title: RSA signing and verification arithmetic
lessons.summary: The public exponent checks a toy signature by recovering the signed number modulo the modulus.
lessons.body:
RSA is the oldest widely used signature algorithm, and its core arithmetic shows clearly why the public key can check a signature without being able to make one.

## A toy RSA signature

The raw RSA private exponentiation resembles the RSA decryption primitive, but real signature encoding is different from encryption padding. For this arithmetic-only example, the signer raises the message's hash to the private exponent, and the signature verifier raises the signature to the public exponent and checks that the hash comes back:

```formula essential
s = h^d mod n
h' = s^e mod n
where
s: the signature, a whole number from 0 to n − 1
h: the message's hash, treated as a whole number smaller than n
d: the private exponent, the secret half of the RSA key; only the signer knows it
e: the public exponent, part of the public key; real keys commonly use 65,537
n: the modulus, the product of two secret primes; part of the public key; NIST guidance uses at least 2,048 bits for RSA signature generation, rather than a toy key
h': the value the signature verifier recovers from the signature; the signature is accepted only if h' equals h
mod: modulo: the remainder after dividing by n (for example, 17 mod 5 = 2)
In words: signing raises the hash to the private power and verifying raises the signature to the public power; the two powers undo each other, so a genuine signature gives back the hash.
```

Notice what each side needs. The signer needs `d`. The verifier needs only the public pair `n` and `e`, and learning them does not reveal `d`, because computing `d` from them is believed to require factoring the modulus.

## Why the two powers undo each other

The key is generated so that the public and private exponents cancel when you count in remainders of a secret number that only someone who knows the two primes can compute.

```formula reference
n = pq
φ = (p − 1)(q − 1)
(ed) mod φ = 1
where
n: the public modulus
p: the first secret prime
q: the second secret prime, distinct from p
φ: phi (Euler's totient of n): how many numbers from 1 to n share no factor with n; computing it needs p and q, so it stays secret
e: the public exponent
d: the private exponent
mod: modulo: the remainder after division
In words: the private exponent is chosen so that, together with the public exponent, it leaves remainder one after dividing by a secret number that only the holder of the two primes can compute; number theory then guarantees that raising a value to one exponent and then the other returns the original value.
```

The classic textbook key uses the primes 61 and 53, giving the public modulus 3233, with public exponent 17 and private exponent 2753. If a message hashes to 65, the signature is 588; raising 588 to the 17th power and keeping the remainder after dividing by 3233 gives 65 again, so the signature verifies.

Anyone can break this tiny example by factoring 3233. Real security needs large keys and a complete, specified signature scheme with proper encoding (the next unit explains why); this lesson only illustrates the verification relationship.

## Key takeaways
- The public exponent checks a toy signature by recovering the signed number modulo the modulus.
- The key exponents are selected to undo one another modulo the secret totient.
- Small keys and raw arithmetic illustrate correctness, never production security.

## Further reading
- [RSA signature schemes — RFC 8017](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017)
- [RSA (cryptosystem) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem))

questions.prompt: A student writes a toy RSA signature verifier. Given the signer's public key (modulus and public exponent), a message hash and a signature, the code raises the **hash** to the public exponent, reduces it modulo the modulus and checks that the result equals the signature. Genuine signatures from the toy signer keep failing. What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing; the check fails because toy keys are too small to verify reliably
options.explanation: Small keys are insecure, but the arithmetic still works exactly for them. A genuine toy signature verifies when the check is done in the right direction.

options.text: The verifier needs the signer's private exponent to check the signature
options.explanation: If verifying needed the private exponent, every verifier could also sign. Public verification without signing power is the whole point of a signature scheme.

options.text: It runs the check backwards: verification raises the signature to the public exponent and compares the result with the hash
options.explanation: Correct. Signing raised the hash to the private exponent; only the public exponent undoes that, so the verifier applies it to the signature and should get the hash back.

options.text: It should decrypt the message with the verifier's own private key first
options.explanation: The verifier's own keys play no part in checking someone else's signature. Only the signer's public key is needed.

questions.workedExample:
1. Signing: the signer raises the hash to the private exponent, modulo the modulus, giving the signature.
2. The public exponent is chosen to undo the private one. So raising the **signature** to the public exponent returns the hash.
3. Raising the **hash** to the public exponent does not undo anything; it produces an unrelated number, so it will not match the signature.
4. Fix: compute the signature to the public exponent, modulo the modulus, and accept only if it equals the hash.

With the classic toy key (modulus 3233, public exponent 17), a hash of 65 has signature 588, and 588 raised to the 17th power modulo 3233 gives 65. The verifier never needs the private exponent; anyone can check, only the key holder can sign. Real schemes add a specified encoding (PSS or PKCS#1 v1.5) before this arithmetic.

lessons.title: Why RSA signatures need encoding
lessons.summary: Raw-message RSA permits signature-first forgery and multiplicative manipulation.
lessons.body:
The previous unit's toy RSA arithmetic verifies correctly, but used on its own it is not a secure signature scheme. This unit shows the two structural weaknesses and the encodings that remove them.

## Why textbook RSA signatures are broken

Raw RSA (the preceding unit's private exponentiation, with no padding) has fatal algebraic structure:

- **Raw-message forgery.** If any number below the modulus counts as a message, an attacker can pick the signature first and compute, from the public key alone, which message it verifies for. If the scheme instead hashes an external message first, this does not by itself find a message with that hash; do not confuse those two models. Neither observation justifies inventing a signature encoding.
- **Multiplication.** Multiplying two valid signatures gives a valid signature on the product of their messages.

The forgery simply runs verification backwards: choose any number as the "signature", raise it to the public exponent, and the result is a message that the pair verifies for. With the toy key (modulus 3233, public exponent 17), the attacker-chosen signature 5 verifies for the message 3086, although the key owner never signed 3086.

```formula reference
m = s^e mod n
where
m: the forged message, a number below n
s: the forged signature: any number the attacker likes
e: the public exponent
n: the public modulus
mod: modulo: the remainder after dividing by n
In words: an attacker can choose any signature value and compute, using only the public key, the raw message it verifies for, so the pair passes verification although the owner never signed it.
```

The multiplication property is the one that makes chosen values possible, and it follows from the ordinary rule for powers:

```formula essential
sig(x) = x^d mod n
(sig(a) sig(b)) mod n = sig(ab)
where
sig: textbook RSA signing with the private exponent, with no padding
x: a raw message representative, a number below n
a: a first message the owner signed
b: a second message the owner signed
d: the private exponent, unknown to the attacker
n: the public modulus
mod: modulo: the remainder after dividing by n
In words: two raw signatures multiplied together (and reduced modulo n) are a valid signature on the two messages multiplied together, so an attacker who holds signatures can combine them into new ones without the private key.
```

With the toy key, an attacker holding the owner's raw signatures on 2 and 3 obtains a valid signature on 6. A forged message such as 3086 may be meaningless, but the security goal (EUF-CMA) counts any new valid pair as a break, and multiplication can produce values the attacker chose.

## Encoding fixes the structure

Real RSA therefore **pads** the hash into a structured, full-width number first, so the product of two encodings is not the encoding of anything:

- **PKCS#1 v1.5** padding: deterministic and used in existing protocols. Secure for signatures if verified strictly, but sloppy parsers have led to forgeries such as Bleichenbacher's 2006 attack on keys with public exponent 3.
- **RSA-PSS**: randomised padding with a security proof. TLS 1.3 requires PSS when RSA signs the handshake (CertificateVerify); PKCS#1 v1.5 is still allowed for the signatures inside certificates.

The practical rule is to call a library's complete signature scheme (for example RSA-PSS with SHA-256) and never feed raw numbers to an RSA "sign" primitive.

## Key takeaways
- Raw-message RSA permits signature-first forgery and multiplicative manipulation.
- An attack on raw message representatives is distinct from finding a preimage for an external hash.
- Use a specified scheme: TLS 1.3 requires RSA-PSS for RSA CertificateVerify signatures.

## Further reading
- [RSA signature schemes — RFC 8017](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017)
- [Probabilistic signature scheme — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_signature_scheme)

questions.prompt: A legacy device signs each numeric instruction code with raw (unpadded) RSA: the signature is the code raised to the private exponent, modulo the public modulus. An attacker has captured the device's signatures on two instruction codes, but not the private key. Which risk does this design create, and what is the fix?

options.text: None: without the private exponent nobody can produce a new valid signature
options.explanation: That is true for a properly encoded scheme, not for raw RSA. Raw RSA's algebra lets signatures be combined without the private exponent.

options.text: Multiplying the two captured signatures (modulo the modulus) gives a valid signature on the product of the two codes; use a specified encoding such as RSA-PSS
options.explanation: Correct. Raw RSA signatures multiply: the product of the signatures is the signature of the product. Padding into a structured, full-width encoding destroys this relationship.

options.text: Adding the two signatures gives a valid signature on the sum of the codes; use a longer key
options.explanation: RSA's structure is multiplicative, not additive. A longer key does not change the algebra either; only proper encoding does.

options.text: The attacker can recover the private exponent from two signatures; switch to ECDSA
options.explanation: Raw RSA signatures do not reveal the private exponent. (Recovering a key from two signatures is the ECDSA nonce-reuse failure, a different problem.)

questions.workedExample:
1. Raw RSA signing is just a power: the signature of x is x raised to the private exponent, modulo the modulus.
2. Powers multiply: raising two numbers to the same power and multiplying the results gives the same answer as multiplying the numbers first and then raising the product. So the signature on one code times the signature on the other, reduced modulo the modulus, is a valid signature on the product of the two codes.
3. The attacker never needs the private exponent; any new valid message–signature pair counts as a forgery, and here the attacker can steer which value is forged.
4. Raw RSA also allows signature-first forgery: pick any number as the signature and compute, from the public key, the message it verifies for.
5. Fix: never sign raw numbers. Use a complete signature scheme that hashes and encodes the message first (RSA-PSS, or strictly verified PKCS#1 v1.5). The encoding of a product is not the product of the encodings, so the trick fails.

(With the textbook key of modulus 3233, the raw signatures on 2 and 3 multiply to a valid raw signature on 6.)

questions.prompt: You are choosing the RSA padding for a new protocol where RSA keys sign handshake transcripts, as TLS 1.3 does in CertificateVerify. Which choice matches TLS 1.3, and why?

options.text: PKCS#1 v1.5, because it is deterministic and therefore easier to test
options.explanation: Determinism is not the deciding factor, and TLS 1.3 does not allow v1.5 for handshake signatures. v1.5 survives mainly in certificate signatures for compatibility.

options.text: OAEP, because it is the modern RSA padding
options.explanation: OAEP is the padding for RSA *encryption*. Signatures use PSS.

options.text: Textbook RSA, since the transcript hash already randomises the input
options.explanation: Raw RSA on arbitrary integer messages is forgeable; the security of a hash-based encoding needs its own precise analysis. Use a specified RSA signature scheme rather than assuming any transcript hash is sufficient.

options.text: RSA-PSS, because its randomised padding has a security proof and TLS 1.3 requires it for handshake signatures
options.explanation: Correct. TLS 1.3 requires RSASSA-PSS for CertificateVerify. PKCS#1 v1.5 is still permitted for signatures *in* certificates.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate the two RSA paddings: OAEP is for encryption, PSS for signatures. That rules out OAEP.
2. Textbook RSA is out: it allows forgery from nothing and multiplication.
3. PKCS#1 v1.5 signatures are deterministic and secure only if parsed strictly; lax parsers enabled Bleichenbacher's 2006 forgery against keys with public exponent 3.
4. PSS adds a random salt and has security analyses under explicit RSA and hash-model assumptions.
5. RFC 8446 requires RSA-PSS for TLS 1.3 handshake signatures, while still allowing v1.5 in certificates issued by CAs.

lessons.title: ECDSA and secret nonce reuse
lessons.summary: An ECDSA signature combines the message hash, private key and per-signature secret nonce.
lessons.body:
ECDSA is an elliptic-curve signature scheme widely used in TLS certificates, passkeys and cryptocurrency wallets. Its security depends on one per-signature secret that is easy to get wrong.

## ECDSA and the nonce

ECDSA signs using an elliptic-curve key. Each signature needs a secret nonce selected according to the scheme, either securely at random or with a specified deterministic derivation. The signature is a pair of numbers:

```formula essential
r = x(kG) mod n
s = (k^{−1}(h + rd)) mod n
where
r: the first half of the signature: the x-coordinate of the curve point kG, reduced modulo n
s: the second half of the signature
k: the secret per-signature nonce, a number from 1 to n − 1; it must not leak, be biased or repeat for different messages
G: the generator: a fixed, public starting point on the elliptic curve
kG: elliptic-curve scalar multiplication: adding the point G to itself k times; easy to compute, infeasible to reverse
x: "the x-coordinate of" a point on the curve
h: the message hash, as a number (its leftmost bits if the hash is longer than n)
d: the signer's private key, a secret number; the public key is the point dG
n: the order of G, a large prime (about 2^256 for P-256)
k^{−1}: the modular inverse of k: the number that gives remainder 1 when multiplied by k, modulo n
mod: modulo: the remainder after dividing by n
In words: r is a public fingerprint of the secret nonce, and s mixes the nonce, the hash and the private key, so anyone who learns the nonce for one signature can solve s for the private key.
```

A signature verifier with the public key checks the pair without learning k or d.

The nonce is the weak point:

- **Reuse `k` for two messages** and anyone can solve two equations for `k`, then for your private key `d`. Sony's PlayStation 3 used a constant `k` for its firmware-signing key; in 2010 the fail0verflow team recovered the key and could sign anything.
- **Certain nonce biases or partial leaks** can enable private-key recovery with enough signatures; exploitability depends on the bias and observations. In 2013 a flaw in Android's `SecureRandom` let attackers steal Bitcoin from wallets that had repeated nonces.

Here is why reuse is fatal. Two signatures with the same k share the same r, and each s gives one equation. Two equations expose two unknowns: subtracting them cancels the private-key term and reveals k, and putting k back into either equation reveals d. Everything else in the equations is public.

```formula reference
s_1 k ≡ h_1 + rd   (mod n)
s_2 k ≡ h_2 + rd   (mod n)
k ≡ (h_1 − h_2) / (s_1 − s_2)   (mod n)
d ≡ (s_1 k − h_1) / r   (mod n)
where
s_1: the s half of the first signature, public
s_2: the s half of the second signature, public
h_1: the hash of the first message, public
h_2: the hash of the second message, public; it must differ from h_1
r: the r half, identical in both signatures because k repeated
k: the reused nonce, secret until this calculation
d: the private key
n: the order of the curve's generator, about 2^256 for P-256
mod: modulo: every step is done in remainders after dividing by n
/: division modulo n: multiplying by the modular inverse of the divisor
≡: congruence: both sides leave the same remainder modulo n
In words: two signatures made with the same nonce over different hashes give two equations; subtracting them reveals the nonce, and the nonce then reveals the private key, using only public values.
```

This needs the two hash values to differ (so the subtraction does not cancel to zero); signing the same message twice with the same nonce just repeats the signature and leaks nothing new.

One standard option is **deterministic ECDSA** (RFC 6979), deriving k from the private key and message hash. It removes reliance on fresh signing-time randomness, but is not a mathematical uniqueness guarantee across all messages. Secure randomness is still needed for key generation, and side-channel/fault defenses remain necessary.

## Key takeaways
- An ECDSA signature combines the message hash, private key and per-signature secret nonce.
- Reusing a nonce for suitable distinct hashes exposes the nonce and then the signing key.
- RFC 6979 derives nonces deterministically but still needs secure key generation and side-channel protection.

## Further reading
- [Deterministic ECDSA — RFC 6979](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6979)
- [Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_Curve_Digital_Signature_Algorithm)

questions.prompt: An ECDSA signer uses the same secret nonce and the same key for two signatures over two different message hashes (distinct modulo the curve's prime group order, so the two signatures' s values differ). Given those signatures and messages, what can an attacker recover?

options.text: Nothing useful; the nonce is secret and never appears in the signature
options.explanation: The nonce is secret, but two signatures with the same nonce share the same r value and give two linear equations in two unknowns: the nonce and the private key.

options.text: Only replay the two existing images on other devices
options.explanation: Replay was possible anyway. The far bigger problem is that the key itself is exposed.

options.text: Recover the nonce, then the private key, and sign arbitrary firmware
options.explanation: Correct. With equal r values, subtracting the two signing equations reveals the nonce, and either equation then gives the private key (worked example). This is how fail0verflow recovered Sony's PS3 signing key in 2010.

options.text: Decrypt the firmware images
options.explanation: Signatures do not encrypt anything; there is nothing to decrypt. The leak is the signing key.

questions.workedExample:
Each ECDSA signature is a pair (r, s). The r half depends only on the secret nonce k, and the s half ties k, the message hash and the private key d together, so two signatures with the same nonce share the same r.

1. Write each signing equation multiplied through by the nonce k. Each one says that s times k equals the hash plus r times the private key d, counted modulo the group order n.
2. The two equations share the same unknown nonce, the same r and the same unknown d. Subtracting one from the other cancels the r-times-d term, leaving the difference of the two s values times k equal to the difference of the two hashes.
3. Dividing (multiplying by a modular inverse) gives k from public values alone.
4. Putting k back into either equation leaves d as the only unknown, so it can be solved too.

Both signatures, both hashes and the shared r are public, so a few lines of modular arithmetic give the private key. The fix is fresh, unbiased nonces, or deterministic nonces via RFC 6979 or Ed25519.

The stated distinct hashes make the difference of the two s values nonzero, so its inverse exists. Repeating a signature on the same message does not provide this independent equation.

lessons.title: Ed25519 and signature format choices
lessons.summary: Ed25519 signing is deterministic and needs no fresh random per-signature nonce.
lessons.body:
The RSA and ECDSA units showed two ways a signature scheme can be misused: raw encodings and bad nonces. Newer designs try to remove those choices from the developer altogether.

## Ed25519: designed to be hard to misuse

**Ed25519** (EdDSA on the Edwards-form edwards25519 curve, RFC 8032) bakes these lessons in:

- The nonce is computed from a secret and the message by a fixed rule. Same key and message, same signature; no fresh per-signature RNG input is required. Key generation still needs secure randomness.
- Its design supports efficient constant-time implementations, with small keys and signatures. Choose a maintained implementation; the scheme does not make every implementation side-channel safe.
- There are fewer parameters to get wrong. You do not pick a hash or a padding scheme.

```python
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives \
    .asymmetric import ed25519
from cryptography import exceptions

# Generate a fresh secret signing key.
sk = ed25519.Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()
pk = sk.public_key()

msg = b"pay alice 10 GBP"
# Sign these exact bytes, not ciphertext.
sig = sk.sign(msg)
print(len(sig))          # 64

# Success returns without an exception.
pk.verify(sig, msg)      # no exception
# The same signature rejects changed data.
try:
    pk.verify(sig, b"pay alice 99 GBP")
except exceptions.InvalidSignature:
    print("rejected")
print(sk.sign(msg) == sig)  # True
```

The last line prints `True` because Ed25519 is deterministic. ECDSA with independently random nonces would normally print False; deterministic ECDSA can instead repeat the signature for the same key and message.

## Choosing an algorithm

| Scheme | Public key | Signature | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| RSA-2048 | 256 B modulus plus exponent/encoding | 256 B | Cost depends on exponent and implementation |
| ECDSA P-256 | 65 B uncompressed SEC1; 33 B compressed | 64 B (r then s, 32 B each) | Needs a correctly generated nonce |
| Ed25519 | 32 B | 64 B | Deterministic, fast |
| ML-DSA-44 | 1,312 B | 2,420 B | Post-quantum |

Sizes depend on encoding: DER ECDSA signatures vary, commonly around 70–72 bytes for P-256; smaller encodings can occur. Ed25519 is a useful choice when the protocol supports it. ECDSA P-256 is widely interoperable, but FIPS 186-5 also specifies EdDSA; compliance depends on a validated implementation and applicable policy. WebAuthn support depends on negotiated algorithms and authenticators. Post-quantum signatures are covered later.

## Key takeaways
- Ed25519 signing is deterministic and needs no fresh random per-signature nonce.
- A modified message fails verification even when the original signature remains unchanged.
- Compare protocol support, validated implementations and actual encodings rather than key sizes alone.

## Further reading
- [EdDSA — RFC 8032](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032)
- [Ed25519 signing — pyca/cryptography docs](https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/asymmetric/ed25519/)

questions.prompt:
What does this code print with overwhelming probability, using the indicated random-nonce ECDSA mode?

```python
m = b"hello"
# Ed25519 repeats for these same bytes.
e1 = ed_key.sign(m)
e2 = ed_key.sign(m)
# ECDSA P-256 with random k
c1 = ec_key.sign(m, ecdsa_sha256)
c2 = ec_key.sign(m, ecdsa_sha256)
# Compare signature bytes, not keys.
print(e1 == e2, c1 == c2)
```

options.text: `True True`
options.explanation: Ed25519 is deterministic, but standard ECDSA uses a fresh random nonce per signature, so its signatures differ each time.

options.text: `False False`
options.explanation: Ed25519 derives its nonce from a secret and the message, so signing the same message twice gives identical bytes.

options.text: `False True`
options.explanation: This has the two schemes the wrong way round.

options.text: `True False`
options.explanation: Correct. Ed25519 is deterministic by design. ECDSA with a random `k` produces a different `(r, s)` each time, yet both verify.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ed25519 computes its nonce as a hash of a secret prefix derived from the key, and the message. Same key and message, same nonce, same signature: `e1 == e2`.
2. ECDSA as used here picks a random `k` per call. Different `k` gives different `r` and `s`: `c1 != c2`.
3. Both ECDSA signatures still verify; a signature scheme can have many valid signatures per message.

(ECDSA with RFC 6979 deterministic nonces would print `True` for both, but that is not the default here.)

questions.prompt: An embedded signer has a securely generated, protected long-term key, but its signing-time RNG is weak. Which choices remove dependence on fresh random per-signature nonces, assuming correct side-channel-resistant implementations? Select all that apply.

options.text: Derive the nonce from the key and message hash by a fixed rule (RFC 6979)
options.explanation: Correct. RFC 6979 derives the nonce from secret key material and the message hash, avoiding this signing-time RNG dependency. It does not eliminate weak key-generation or side-channel failures.

options.text: Switch to Ed25519, which derives its nonce from a secret and the message
options.explanation: Correct. Ed25519 does not request a fresh random nonce for each signature. Secure key generation and implementation defenses are still necessary.

options.text: Use SHA-512 instead of SHA-256 for the message hash
options.explanation: The nonce is a separate value from the message hash. A weak or repeated `k` leaks the key whatever hash is used.

options.text: Keep using random nonces but only sign a few messages a day
options.explanation: Fewer signatures are not a reliable fix. Reuse for two distinct hash representatives can recover the key; biased-nonce attacks depend on the bias and available observations.

options.text: Encrypt the signatures before sending them
options.explanation: This hides `(r, s)` from passive observers, but the receiver still sees them and exposure of vulnerable signatures may permit key recovery under the nonce failure. It treats the symptom, not the cause.

questions.workedExample: Deterministic ECDSA derives its nonce from the private key and message hash; Ed25519 derives a nonce from a secret-derived prefix and message. These designs remove reliance on fresh signing-time entropy, but secure key generation and side-channel/fault resistance still matter. Repeated nonces on suitable distinct hashes can reveal an ECDSA private key from two signatures. Rate limits do not repair that underlying flaw; exploitability of bias depends on its structure and observations.

lessons.title: Using signatures safely in applications
lessons.summary: Use the exact signed bytes after verification, including in structured document handlers.
lessons.body:
A signature check answers one narrow question: were these exact bytes signed by the private key matching this public key? Most real failures come from the code around that check.

## Where signatures are used

- **TLS**: a CA signs the server's certificate, and the server signs the handshake (in the certificate and TLS units).
- **Software updates and packages**: apt, Windows Authenticode, Apple code signing, Android APKs, and Sigstore for open-source artefacts.
- **Git**: signed commits and tags, with GPG or SSH keys.
- **Tokens**: JWTs signed with RS256, ES256 or EdDSA, so any service can verify without the issuer's secret.
- **Email**: DKIM validates selected headers and body content against a signing domain's key. The signing domain need not match the visible From address; DMARC alignment is a separate check.
- **Passkeys**: WebAuthn assertions sign authenticator data plus a client-data hash that binds the challenge and origin. Some passkeys synchronize between devices; device-bound and backed-up credentials have different custody models.

## Pitfalls

- **Check what was actually signed.** XML Signature "wrapping" attacks moved the signed element and inserted an unsigned one that the application then read. Sign canonical bytes, and act only on the bytes you verified.
- **Do not let the message choose the algorithm.** Early JWT libraries trusted the token's `alg` header, so `alg: none` or switching RS256 to HS256 (using the public key as an HMAC secret) bypassed verification. Pin the expected algorithm.
- **A signature proves the key, not the person.** Binding a public key to an identity is a separate problem, solved by certificates.
- **Compromised keys can create new forgeries.** Trusted timestamps or other reliable prior records can help distinguish older signatures. Whether an old artifact remains acceptable depends on the earliest plausible compromise, trust-chain validation and policy, not a universal timestamp rule.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A pass that tells the guard how to check it
> Imagine a building pass with a printed note: "Holder of this pass needs no photo check." A guard who follows instructions printed on the pass itself will wave through anyone who prints that note on a home-made card.
>
> **How it maps:** A JWT's `alg` header is that printed note. A verifier that reads `alg` from the token lets the attacker choose `none`, or choose HMAC and use the published RSA public key as the shared secret. A guard with a fixed procedure for each kind of pass is a verifier configured with the allowed algorithm for each key.
>
> **Where it stops:** A guard can use judgement and spot an odd-looking pass. Software does exactly what the code says, so the protection must be an explicit allow-list in the verification call, not an expectation that bad tokens will look suspicious.

## Verifying a JWT safely

RFC 8725 (the JWT Best Current Practices) turns these failures into rules. A relying service should:

1. **Fix the algorithm per key.** The library must let the caller list the allowed algorithms and must reject anything else; each key is used with exactly one algorithm. `none` should never be accepted for a token that is meant to be signed.
2. **Choose the key from its own configuration**, not from the token. A `kid` header may select among keys you already trust, but must be validated before it is used in a lookup. Do not follow a `jku` or `x5u` URL from the token without an allow-list of locations; fetching arbitrary URLs invites server-side request forgery.
3. **Check the claims after the signature**: the issuer (`iss`) must own the verifying key, the audience (`aud`) must be this service, and the expiry (`exp`) must not have passed.
4. **Remember a signed token is readable.** A JWS payload is only encoded, so never put secrets in it.

## Key takeaways
- Use the exact signed bytes after verification, including in structured document handlers.
- Enforce the expected algorithm and trusted key, then check issuer, audience and expiry, instead of trusting token headers.
- Key identity, compromise timing and relying-party policy remain separate from signature mathematics.

## Further reading
- [RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725)
- [Critical vulnerabilities in JSON Web Token libraries — Auth0](https://auth0.com/blog/critical-vulnerabilities-in-json-web-token-libraries/)
- [SAML Security Cheat Sheet — OWASP](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SAML_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [Digital signature — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_signature)

questions.prompt: A service verifies JWTs signed with RS256 using a library call `verify(token, key=public_key_pem)`, letting the library read the algorithm from the token header. An attacker sends a token with `"alg": "HS256"` and a valid HMAC computed using the public key PEM as the secret. What happens, and what is the fix?

options.text: Rejected, because HMAC can't use a public key
options.explanation: An HMAC accepts any byte string as a key, including the PEM text of a public key, which the attacker can download.

options.text: Accepted by a vulnerable library, because it trusts the header's algorithm; pin the expected algorithm to RS256
options.explanation: Correct. The library switches to HMAC and uses the 'key' it was given (the public key) as the shared secret, which the attacker also knows. Never let the message choose how it is verified.

options.text: Accepted, and the fix is to use a 4096-bit RSA key
options.explanation: Key size is irrelevant: RSA is never used in the forged path.

options.text: Rejected, because the payload is encrypted
options.explanation: JWS tokens are signed, not encrypted. The payload is base64url, readable by anyone.

questions.workedExample:
1. The library sees `alg: HS256` and computes `HMAC(key, header.payload)`.
2. The `key` it was handed is the RSA public key PEM, which is public.
3. The attacker computed the same HMAC with the same PEM, so the tags match.
4. The token is accepted with whatever claims the attacker wrote.

Fix: `verify(token, key, algorithms=["RS256"])`, or use a library that binds the algorithm to the key. The same mistake allowed `alg: none` tokens.

questions.prompt: A SAML handler verifies a signature referencing one Assertion by ID, then uses a separate unscoped query that selects the first Assertion's NameID. Assume it performs no protective schema/uniqueness checks. An attacker inserts an unsigned Assertion before the signed one. What can go wrong?

options.text: Verification passes on the signed assertion, but the lookup returns the attacker's unsigned one, so the attacker logs in as anyone
options.explanation: Correct. This is XML Signature Wrapping: verify one thing, act on another. The fix is to act only on the exact element (bytes) that was verified.

options.text: The XML parser rejects duplicate elements
options.explanation: XML syntax permits repeated elements, though schema and protocol validation may reject a particular structure. The prompt stipulates that this handler omits those protections.

options.text: Nothing; the signature check fails because the document changed
options.explanation: The signature covers only the referenced element. Adding a sibling elsewhere leaves that element, and its signature, intact.

options.text: The attacker can now recover the IdP's private key
options.explanation: Nothing about the key leaks; the bug is in what the application reads after verification.

questions.workedExample:
1. The signature references the signed assertion by ID, and verifying it succeeds.
2. The lookup is a separate query over the whole document. It finds the *first* `<Assertion>`, which is the attacker's.
3. So the security check and the business logic look at different data.
4. Rule: after verifying, use only the verified data: hand the verified element on, or the canonical bytes that were checked. Do not run a separate unscoped selection over the original document; consume the verified element or validated representation.

questions.prompt: A code-signing key may have leaked as early as January. Which independent evidence could support distinguishing releases signed before that earliest plausible compromise, subject to validation and relying-party policy?

options.text: Nothing; every signature from that key must be distrusted
options.explanation: Without independent timing evidence, verification alone cannot distinguish pre-compromise releases. Acceptance depends on the available evidence and policy.

options.text: Releases whose signatures were countersigned by a trusted timestamping authority before January
options.explanation: A valid trusted timestamp predating the earliest plausible compromise supports prior existence of the signed artifact. It is not automatic proof of legitimate authorship; key custody, chain status and policy still matter.

options.text: Re-verify the old signatures with the public key
options.explanation: They will verify perfectly. So would signatures the attacker creates now, with any date they like.

options.text: Switch to Ed25519, which makes past signatures safe
options.explanation: Changing algorithm protects future signatures only. It says nothing about which past signatures were made by the company rather than an attacker.

questions.workedExample: A compromised key can create valid new signatures with attacker-controlled dates. RFC3161 timestamps bind a message imprint and trusted time in a signed timestamp token. A validated timestamp before the earliest plausible compromise can support acceptance of an older artifact under the applicable policy. Other reliable prior records may also help. Revoke/replace the affected signing credential and investigate the actual compromise interval; revocation date and invalidity date are distinct fields, not an instruction to backdate a CRL entry.

lessons.title: Certificate trust chains and fields
lessons.summary: Certificates bind names to public keys under a trusted issuer and policy.
lessons.body:
Public verification leaves an identity-binding gap. A signature proves that a message was made by the holder of some private key. It does not tell you *whose* key it is. If an attacker can hand you their public key and say "this is bank.com", every signature check passes and you are talking to the attacker.

A **certificate** closes that gap. It is a small signed document that says "this public key belongs to this name", signed by someone you already trust. A **public key infrastructure** (PKI) is everything around that: who is allowed to sign certificates, how they check identities, how trust is distributed, and how mistakes are undone.

## The idea: a chain of signatures

You cannot check every server's key in person. Instead you trust a small set of **root certificate authorities** (CAs), whose public keys ship with your operating system or browser. Each root vouches for a few **intermediate CAs**, which vouch for millions of websites.

```
Root CA        (in your trust store,
   |            key kept offline)
   | signs
   v
Intermediate   (online, issues certs)
   |
   | signs
   v
Leaf: shop.example.com + public key
```

Trust follows a **valid certification path**, not signatures alone: validity, constraints, permitted uses and relying-party policy must also pass. A correctly configured server sends the leaf and required intermediates; the client already has the trust anchor.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A passport and the issuing government
> A border officer has never met you, but accepts your passport because it was issued by a government the officer recognises, using security features the officer knows how to check. The officer then compares the name and photo with the person standing there.
>
> **How it maps:** The passport is the certificate: it binds a name to something only the holder can produce (here, signatures from the private key). The government is the CA, and the officer's list of recognised governments is the trust store of root CAs. A passport office acting for the government resembles an intermediate CA, and the officer's checks of validity dates and restrictions resemble path validation.
>
> **Where it stops:** A passport photo is matched by eye, while a certificate is checked by verifying signatures and then proving possession of the private key in a protocol such as TLS; a photocopied certificate is useless without that key. Certificates also carry machine-checked limits (Basic Constraints, key usage, name constraints) that have no clean passport equivalent.

Why not let roots sign leaves directly? Replacing a widely distributed trust anchor can be operationally difficult because many relying parties need updated trust stores. So roots live in hardware security modules, often in offline vaults, and come out only to sign a new intermediate or a revocation list. If an intermediate is compromised, the root revokes it and signs a new one.

## Inside an X.509 certificate

Web certificates use the **X.509 v3** format (profiled in RFC 5280), encoded in ASN.1 DER and usually shown as base64 "PEM". The signed part is called the **TBSCertificate** ("to be signed"):

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Serial number | `04:3f:a1:...` (unique per CA) |
| Issuer | `CN=Toy Issuing CA` |
| Validity | not before / not after |
| Subject | `CN=shop.example.com` |
| Public key | EC P-256, 65 bytes |
| Extensions | see below |

After the TBS bytes come the signature algorithm and the CA's signature over them. Changing the signed subject or key bytes without a new valid signature causes verification to fail, under the scheme’s security assumptions.

The **extensions** carry most of the security meaning:

- **Subject Alternative Name (SAN)**: the DNS names (or IPs) the certificate is valid for, such as `shop.example.com` and `*.cdn.example.com`. Browsers match only against SAN; RFC 9525 says the Common Name must not be used to identify a service, and a wildcard matches exactly one leftmost label.
- **Basic Constraints**: `CA:TRUE` or `CA:FALSE`, plus an optional `pathLenConstraint` limiting the number of non-self-issued intermediate CA certificates below it in a valid path (not leaf certificates).
- **Key Usage / Extended Key Usage**: what the key may do, such as `keyCertSign` for a CA, or `serverAuth` and `clientAuth` for leaves.
- **Name Constraints**: limits a CA to certain namespaces, for example only names under `.corp.example.com`.
- **Authority Information Access**: where to download the issuer's certificate and where its OCSP responder lives.
- **CRL Distribution Points**: where to fetch the revocation list.
- **SCT list**: signed promises of timely inclusion in Certificate Transparency logs; an SCT is not itself a Merkle inclusion proof.

> [!warning] Basic Constraints is not optional
> In 2002, Moxie Marlinspike showed that Internet Explorer did not check Basic Constraints. Anyone with an ordinary leaf certificate could use it as a CA and sign a valid-looking certificate for any site. Microsoft documented the missing Basic Constraints checks in MS02-050; path authorization is separate from signature validity.

## Key takeaways
- Certificates bind names to public keys under a trusted issuer and policy.
- Roots anchor trust; intermediates permit routine issuance while restricting root-key use.
- SAN, Basic Constraints, key usage and name constraints add security meaning beyond a valid signature.

## Further reading
- [X.509 certificate profile — RFC 5280](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280)
- [Service identity in TLS — RFC 9525](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9525)

questions.prompt: What problem does a certificate solve that a digital signature alone does not?

options.text: It encrypts the public key so attackers cannot read it
options.explanation: Public keys are meant to be public. Certificates are sent in full and encrypting the key would serve no purpose.

options.text: It makes signatures faster to verify
options.explanation: Certificates add verification work: the client checks the CA's signatures as well.

options.text: It binds a public key to an identity (a name), vouched for by a CA the client already trusts
options.explanation: Correct. A signature proves a message came from some key's holder; the certificate tells you whose key it is.

options.text: It replaces the private key so the server does not need one
options.explanation: The server still needs its private key to prove it owns the certificate's public key, for example by signing the TLS handshake.

questions.workedExample:
1. A signature check answers: was this made with the private key matching public key P?
2. It does not answer: is P really bank.com's key? An attacker can generate their own pair and claim the name.
3. A certificate is a trusted third party's signature over (name, P).
4. If you trust that CA's key, you can trust the binding, and then the signature check means something.

questions.prompt: Why do CAs issue website certificates from intermediate CAs rather than directly from their root?

options.text: Intermediates allow routine issuance while restricting root-key use; recovering from an intermediate compromise requires replacing it and ensuring relying parties reject it
options.explanation: Correct. Isolation can protect the trust anchor, but revocation distribution, certificate replacement and client enforcement remain operational work.

options.text: Intermediates make the chain shorter for clients
options.explanation: An intermediate adds a certificate to the chain. The benefit is security, not size.

options.text: Root keys cannot produce signatures that browsers accept on leaves
options.explanation: Roots can sign leaves technically; RFC 5280 does not forbid it. It is a key-protection policy, not a format limit.

options.text: Intermediates are required for RSA but not for ECDSA
options.explanation: The hierarchy is independent of the signature algorithm.

questions.workedExample: An intermediate can be replaced under an existing trusted root, but clients must reject the compromised issuer and affected leaves may need replacement. A compromised root can require updating many trust stores. Both recoveries can be costly; keeping a root offline with restricted use reduces exposure, rather than making intermediate compromise cheap or harmless.

questions.prompt: A certificate has subject `CN=www.shop.com` and a Subject Alternative Name list containing only `shop.com`. A browser connects to `https://www.shop.com`. What happens?

options.text: It succeeds, because the Common Name matches
options.explanation: Browsers ignore the Common Name for hostname matching and use only the SAN extension.

options.text: It succeeds, but shows a warning icon
options.explanation: A hostname mismatch is a hard failure in browsers, not a cosmetic warning.

options.text: It succeeds, because `shop.com` covers all its subdomains
options.explanation: A DNS name in SAN matches exactly. Covering subdomains needs a wildcard entry, and even `*.shop.com` matches one level only.

options.text: It fails with a name mismatch, because only SAN is checked and `shop.com` does not cover `www.shop.com`
options.explanation: Correct. The existing SAN does not cover www.shop.com. Add that exact SAN or an applicable *.shop.com wildcard.

questions.workedExample:
1. Modern clients (browsers since around 2017) match the hostname only against SAN `dNSName` entries.
2. The SAN list is `[shop.com]`.
3. `www.shop.com` ≠ `shop.com`, and there is no wildcard.
4. So validation fails. The fix is to request both names in the CSR: `shop.com` and `www.shop.com`.

questions.prompt: An employee obtains an ordinary leaf certificate for `blog.example.org` (with `CA:FALSE`) and uses its private key to sign a certificate for `bank.com`. A client receives the chain `bank.com ← blog.example.org ← intermediate ← root`. Every signature verifies. What should stop this?

options.text: Nothing; if every signature verifies, the chain is valid
options.explanation: Signatures are only one check. This is exactly the bug Moxie Marlinspike found in Internet Explorer in 2002.

options.text: Certificate Transparency logs refuse the forged certificate
options.explanation: CT would make issuance visible if submitted, but the forger simply would not log it. Browsers might reject the missing SCTs, but the fundamental check is Basic Constraints.

options.text: The client checks Basic Constraints: `blog.example.org` is not a CA, so it cannot issue certificates
options.explanation: Correct. The proposed intermediate explicitly has CA:FALSE, so a proper path validator rejects it. Key Usage and other constraints are additional applicable checks.

options.text: The hostname check fails because `bank.com` doesn't match `blog.example.org`
options.explanation: The client checks the hostname against the *leaf*, which here says `bank.com`. That check passes.

questions.workedExample:
Walk the validation checklist for the chain:

1. Signatures: all verify. Pass.
2. Dates: assume valid. Pass.
3. Every issuer must be a CA. The issuer of `bank.com` is `blog.example.org`, which has `CA:FALSE`. **Fail.**
4. Hostname vs leaf SAN: `bank.com`. Would pass.

Step 3 is what makes leaf keys unable to mint certificates. Clients that skipped it (IE in 2002, several later TLS libraries) accepted forged chains.

lessons.title: Issuing certificates with ACME
lessons.summary: A CSR demonstrates possession of the requested public key’s private half; domain control needs its own validation.
lessons.body:
A certificate is only as trustworthy as the checks the CA made before signing it. For ordinary web certificates, those checks are automated checks of control over a domain name.

## Getting a certificate

1. You generate a key pair. Protect the private key; where it is generated, backed up or used depends on the deployment and key-management service.
2. You create a **certificate signing request** (CSR, PKCS#10): your public key and requested names, *signed with your private key*. That signature proves you hold the key.
3. The CA validates that you control the names.
4. The CA signs a certificate and you install it with the intermediate chain.

For the web, step 3 is **domain validation** (DV), and **ACME** (RFC 8555) is one widely used automation protocol. It was developed through the IETF, with Let's Encrypt as an early deployment. The CA gives you a random token and checks you can publish it:

| Challenge | Proof of control |
|---|---|
| HTTP-01 | Serve key authorization under `/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token>` |
| DNS-01 | Publish a digest of key authorization under `_acme-challenge.<name>` |
| TLS-ALPN-01 | Present a special cert on port 443 |

For Let's Encrypt wildcard requests, use DNS-01. Control of the delegated challenge record can satisfy this validation; it need not give control of every record in the entire zone. Organisation Validation (OV) and Extended Validation (EV) add legal-entity validation requirements. They do not inherently provide stronger encryption than DV; actual cryptographic strength depends on the chosen keys, algorithms and protocol.

Domain validation has a weak spot: it trusts DNS and routing *from the CA's point of view*. An attacker who hijacks a BGP route to your server for a few minutes could pass HTTP-01. CAs now validate from several network vantage points (**multi-perspective validation**): as of October 2026 the Baseline Requirements demand at least four remote perspectives, rising to five from 15 December 2026, with a limited number allowed to disagree. You can also publish a **CAA** DNS record listing which CAs may issue for your domain at all.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A bank posting a code to your address
> To prove you live at an address, a bank posts a one-time code there and asks you to read it back. Anyone who can read the post at that address passes, whoever owns the house.
>
> **How it maps:** HTTP-01 and DNS-01 are the posted code: the CA hands out a token and checks that it appears on your web server or in your DNS. Passing proves control of the name at that moment, not legal ownership. A BGP hijack is like an attacker briefly redirecting the post, which is why CAs now check from several places at once.
>
> **Where it stops:** A letter takes days and is hard to divert; network routes can be changed in seconds and from far away. The CA's check is also bound to your ACME account key, so the response cannot simply be replayed for a different applicant.

## Key takeaways
- A CSR demonstrates possession of the requested public key’s private half; domain control needs its own validation.
- Let’s Encrypt wildcard validation uses DNS-01, including suitable delegated challenge records.
- CAA and multi-perspective validation constrain compliant issuance and localized routing attacks.

## Further reading
- [ACME — RFC 8555](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8555)
- [Challenge types — Let's Encrypt](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/challenge-types/)
- [Baseline Requirements — CA/Browser Forum](https://cabforum.org/working-groups/server/baseline-requirements/requirements/)

questions.prompt: You want a Let's Encrypt certificate for `*.apps.example.com`. Your web servers are behind a load balancer and you can edit DNS through an API. Which ACME challenge must you use?

options.text: HTTP-01, serving the token from one of the web servers
options.explanation: HTTP-01 proves control of one host name. Let's Encrypt does not allow it for wildcard certificates.

options.text: DNS-01, publishing a TXT record at `_acme-challenge.apps.example.com`
options.explanation: Correct for Let's Encrypt: wildcard validation uses DNS-01. Control of the challenge record or its delegation is sufficient; whole-zone administration is not inherently required.

options.text: TLS-ALPN-01 on port 443
options.explanation: Like HTTP-01, TLS-ALPN-01 proves control of a single host and cannot be used for wildcards.

options.text: No challenge; wildcards are issued on the basis of the account key
options.explanation: Every name must be validated. The account key identifies you but proves nothing about domain control.

questions.workedExample: For Let's Encrypt, publish the DNS-01 digest derived from the challenge token and account key at _acme-challenge.apps.example.com. A DNS provider API or delegated challenge zone can automate this. Grant narrowly scoped record access where possible: the API credential may enable unauthorized certificate issuance for names it can validate. It need not grant control of the entire parent zone.

questions.prompt: An attacker briefly hijacks the BGP route to your web server's IP range and answers an HTTP-01 challenge for your domain from their own machine. Which defence most directly makes this attack fail at a well-run CA?

options.text: Multi-perspective issuance corroboration: diverse network views can make a localized hijack fail the CA's required quorum
options.explanation: Correct. A hijack affecting too few validation perspectives cannot satisfy quorum. It is not a guarantee that every disagreement prevents issuance or that a sufficiently broad hijack fails.

options.text: OCSP stapling
options.explanation: Stapling concerns revocation status in the handshake; it plays no part in validating a new certificate request.

options.text: HSTS
options.explanation: HSTS tells browsers to use HTTPS. It does nothing to stop a CA being fooled during validation.

options.text: Certificate pinning in browsers
options.explanation: Browsers removed public key pinning (HPKP). It would also only reject the certificate after issuance, not prevent it.

questions.workedExample: HTTP-01 validates the challenge response reached by the CA. Diverse remote perspectives reduce the chance that one localized routing attack controls enough observations. lessons.title: Building and validating certificate paths
lessons.summary: Path building chooses an issuer chain; validation checks signatures, dates, constraints and application identity policy.
lessons.body:
A client receiving a certificate must decide two separate things: is this certificate genuinely issued under a root I trust, and is it a certificate for the server I meant to reach? Skipping either check defeats TLS.

## How a client validates a chain

A client given a leaf and some intermediates must **build a path** to a trusted root, then check every link:

1. Each certificate's signature verifies with the next one's public key.
2. The certificates in the path are within their validity windows. A trust anchor is an input to validation, not necessarily processed as another path certificate; root-certificate expiry handling varies.
3. Intermediate issuers are authorized CAs; Basic Constraints, applicable Key Usage, path-length constraints, name constraints and unrecognized critical extensions are checked.
4. The leaf's SAN matches the hostname, and its EKU allows `serverAuth`.
5. Apply the client's revocation and browser CT policies. Coverage, freshness and failure handling vary; certificate-path validation alone does not establish either.

Path building is harder than it looks, because a CA can have several certificates with the same key: a self-signed root plus **cross-signed** versions issued by older roots, so new CAs work on old devices. On 30 September 2021 the old root that cross-signed Let's Encrypt, DST Root CA X3, expired. Clients with the appropriate trust anchor and usable path building could validate through ISRG Root X1. Other client families handled the cross-sign and trust-anchor expiry according to their own policy; compatibility was not one universal path switch. Some older OpenSSL 1.0.2 configurations selected the expired path and failed, affecting API integrations.

Here is step 1 alone, using the `cryptography` library:

```python
from cryptography import x509

def check_links(chain):
    # chain[0] = leaf, chain[-1] = root
    # Pair each child with its next issuer.
    for c, iss in zip(chain, chain[1:]):
        # raises if the signature is bad
        c.verify_directly_issued_by(iss)
        print(c.subject.rfc4514_string(),
              "<-",
              iss.subject.rfc4514_string())
```

For a root, intermediate and leaf, this prints `CN=shop.test <- CN=Toy Issuing CA` then `CN=Toy Issuing CA <- CN=Toy Root`. `verify_directly_issued_by` checks issuer/subject name agreement and signature validity; this loop does not check dates, hostname, CA constraints, trust, revocation or CT. Use a maintained validator and configure the required policy. `cryptography.x509.verification.PolicyBuilder` can build a server certificate verifier with hostname/path checks, but has no input for live revocation data or browser CT enforcement.

## The hostname check is half of authentication

A valid chain only proves that *some* trusted CA issued the certificate to *somebody*. Anyone can obtain a perfectly valid certificate for a domain they control, such as `attacker.example`. If the client never compares the certificate's names with the name it set out to reach, an attacker on the network can present that genuine certificate and the handshake succeeds.

RFC 9525 describes the check. The client builds its **reference identifier** from what the user or configuration asked for (the hostname in the URL, not a name supplied by the server) and compares it with the DNS names in the certificate's SAN. The Common Name must not be used, a wildcard matches exactly one leftmost label, and an automated client should abort on a mismatch rather than ask anyone.

This failure is easy to create by accident, because many TLS APIs separate the two checks:

- In Python's `ssl` module, `CERT_REQUIRED` validates the chain but *does not* match hostnames; `check_hostname` must also be on. `ssl.create_default_context()` enables both. Code that sets `check_hostname = False` "to fix a test" removes server authentication while still showing an encrypted connection.
- Disabling verification entirely (`verify=False`, `CERT_NONE`, `InsecureSkipVerify: true`) removes both checks at once.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A genuine passport for the wrong person
> You are meeting a solicitor called Priya Patel. Someone hands you a real, government-issued passport and you check every security feature carefully, but you never read the name on it. It belongs to a stranger.
>
> **How it maps:** Checking the passport's security features is chain validation: the certificate really was issued under a trusted root. Reading the name and comparing it with "Priya Patel" is the hostname check: comparing the certificate's SAN with the name you intended to reach. Skipping it accepts any genuine certificate, including one the attacker obtained for their own domain.
>
> **Where it stops:** A person can be questioned further, and a passport has one name. A certificate may list many names, and must also be backed by proof that the server holds the matching private key during the handshake; the comparison is an exact rule set (RFC 9525), not a judgement call.

## Key takeaways
- Path building chooses an issuer chain; validation checks signatures, dates, constraints and application identity policy.
- A trusted chain without a hostname match authenticates nobody in particular; keep hostname checking on.
- Serve required intermediates and allow valid alternative paths when cross-signed roots expire.

## Further reading
- [X.509 certificate profile — RFC 5280](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280)
- [Service identity in TLS — RFC 9525](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9525)
- [ssl — TLS/SSL wrapper — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ssl.html)
- [X.509 verification — pyca/cryptography docs](https://cryptography.io/en/latest/x509/verification/)
- [DST Root CA X3 expiration (September 2021) — Let's Encrypt](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/dst-root-ca-x3-expiration-september-2021/)

questions.prompt: A Python service calling an API starts failing with "unable to get local issuer certificate" after the API provider renews its certificate. Chrome loads the API's URL without complaint. What is the most likely cause?

options.explanation: That error means the client could not build a path to a trusted root. Algorithm problems give different errors.

options.text: The certificate has been revoked
options.explanation: Python's `ssl` module does not check revocation by default, and revocation produces a different error.

options.text: Python's clock is wrong
options.explanation: A clock problem shows up as an expired or not-yet-valid certificate, not a missing issuer.

options.text: The provider is serving only the leaf certificate, without the intermediate, and Chrome is filling the gap from its cache or the AIA URL
options.explanation: Correct. Path building fails in clients that do not fetch missing intermediates. The fix is on the server: serve the full chain.

questions.workedExample: A missing intermediate is a common explanation for this symptom, but an absent or different trust anchor can also cause it. Inspect the chain actually served (using the correct SNI hostname) and the failing client's trust store. Some browser/platform combinations retrieve or cache missing issuers; behavior is not universal. Configure the server to send its leaf and necessary intermediates.
